newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 24.

text.p: Commandos struck as rebels played soccer: Peruvian commandos freed 71 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Wednesday after timing the attack to coincide with an indoor soccer game by the Marxist rebel captors. Page 1.

Chinese official tries to smuggle apple cuttings: A member of a visiting Chinese trade delegation was caught at Auckland International Airport trying to smuggle out a new breed of apple trees. Page 1.

Treasury warning over coalition commitments: The $5 billion in extra government spending in the coalition agreement is likely to add to inflation pressure and increase the risks of a change in international sentiment toward New Zealand, according to Treasury advice to the government. Page 2.

Critics voice key concern over super referendum: A compulsory superannuation scheme should not go ahead unless supported by a clear majority in September's referendum, the electoral law select committee was told on Wednesday. Page 2.
Jobs go as Prudential absorbs NZI Life: Prudential has scrapped nearly 150 jobs as it absorbs the operations of NZI Life. Page 13.

TVNZ boosts Government coffers by $62m: Government coffers have been boosted by a $62.4 million dividend from Television New Zealand, which reported a record profit of $60.6 million for 1996 on Wednesday. Page 13.

Bank's data 'worsened slowdown': The economic slowdown in the past year would have been less dramatic if the Reserve Bank had more accurate and timely figures to work with, according to a group of exporters. Page 13.

Customs duty avoider named: Name suppression was lifted in Auckland District Court on Wednesday on clothing importer Colin Henderson, convicted last month of avoiding hundreds and thousands of dollars of customs duty by smuggling garments from Korea and Hong Kong. Page 13.

Mortgage interest rates 'hostage to Government': Mortgage interest rates were hostage to the government's spending proclivities, Countrywide Bank chief executive David Wolfenden said on Wednesday. Page 13.
